fields.meta_title: Timesheet Approval Workflow for Any Approver | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a timesheet approval workflow that sends project hours to their leads, contractor weeks to the client, and incomplete weeks back.
fields.h1: Build a Timesheet Approval Workflow for Every Approver
fields.hero_description: Get a timesheet approval workflow that sends each week of hours to the person who should sign it and logs the decision.
fields.features_heading: The Rules Behind Every Approved Timesheet
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the timesheet form, the routing, and the record from your description of who signs which hours.
fields.feature_1:
Approvers named in plain English

Describe the rule as your operations lead would: hours on a client project go to its lead. Emergent builds the timesheet form and routing from that, and edits both by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Project codes from the tools you use

The app connects to any tool with an API, such as your project tracker or QuickBooks. Project codes and their leads sync in, and each line of hours names the person who approves it.
fields.feature_3:
Checks that run before a manager looks

Write down the checks someone runs by hand today, like an empty workday or a closed project code. The app runs them on submit and returns the week with the problem line marked.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders that reach one person

The app sends Slack, email, and in-app reminders to whoever holds a timesheet right now. A week that sits unsigned past the time you set escalates to the next name on your list.
fields.feature_5:
Every decision kept in your database

Submissions, approvals, returns, and comments live in a database you own. Months later, the record for any week still shows who signed it, when, and the comment they left.
fields.feature_6:
No approver seats to count

Emergent has no per-approver seats and no task cap. Add every project lead and client contact who signs hours as approvers. The free tier covers building and publishing the app.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Weeks of Hours, Four Approvers
fields.tab_content_1:
24 hours to one lead, 16 to another

Imre Tolvanen splits his 40-hour week between two projects. The 24 hours on the Clinic Booking App go to its project lead, Tobiah Mwangi, and the 16 hours on Internal Tools go to Renske Obuya. Tobiah has approved his part. The week counts as approved once Renske signs too.
fields.tab_content_2:
Billing waits for Lowmoor to sign off

Lior Bramwell works on site at Lowmoor Dental Group, placed there by the agency he works for. His 38 hours go to the client contact, Ysolde Kirchner, not to anyone at the agency. Once she approves, the hours sync to your billing tool. Until then, billing sees nothing.
fields.tab_content_3:
Eight missing hours send it back

Kwabena Lisle leaves Thursday blank and submits 32 of his 40 hours, with no leave entry for that day. The app returns the week to him with Thursday marked, before his manager, Ottoline Brandt, sees it. Once he logs the 8 hours or a leave day, it goes to Ottoline.
fields.tab_content_4:
With Henrike out, Rasmus approves seven

Henrike Aldana is out this week, so the 7 timesheets from her team go to the backup she named, Rasmus Ekwueme. He approves all 7. When Henrike is back, the log shows every week Rasmus signed and the comments he left on each.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Timesheet Approval Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to map who signs which hours, then build a timesheet approval workflow with Emergent and test it on past weeks.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write down who approves which hours
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 List the checks before anyone signs
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Name a backup for every approver
fields.howto_step_1_des: Export last month's timesheets to one sheet. Mark the weeks that were sent back, who approved each one, and how many days each waited for a signature.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write down the approver for each kind of hours: the project lead for project codes, the client contact for placed contractors, the manager for the rest.
fields.howto_step_3_des: List what should stop a week before it reaches an approver, such as a workday with no hours and no leave entry, or a project code that has closed.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick a backup for each approver. Decide how long a week can wait before the first reminder, and when it should escalate to the next name.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Describe the rules in plain English. From that prompt, Emergent builds the app: the submission form, each route, the reminders, and a dashboard of open weeks.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Connect your project and billing tools
fields.howto_step_6_des: Connect the project tracker that holds your project codes and the billing or payroll tool that should receive approved hours. Any tool with an API works.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Run two past weeks through the rules
fields.howto_step_7_des: Replay two past weeks and compare each route with the person who signed at the time. Fix any route that sent hours to the wrong person, then publish the app.

faq_plan.q: What is a timesheet approval workflow?
faq_plan.a: A timesheet approval workflow is the path a submitted week of hours takes until someone with authority signs it. It sets who signs which hours and what a week must pass before it reaches them. It also names a stand-in for each approver and where approved hours go next, such as billing or payroll.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a timesheet approval workflow?
faq_plan.a: List the people who sign each kind of hours, the problems that should stop a week, and a stand-in for each approver. Then describe those rules in plain English to Emergent's AI automation builder. It builds the app from that prompt, and you change any rule later by prompting again. Test it on two past weeks before you publish.

faq_plan.q: How should a timesheet approval workflow handle hours split across projects?
faq_plan.a: It should send each project's hours to that project's lead, and the week should count as approved only once every lead has signed their part. If your policy wants one person accountable for the total, add the employee's manager as a final step after the leads. Keep project codes in one list, so each line of hours resolves to exactly one lead.

faq_plan.q: Can a timesheet approval workflow pass approved hours to a billing tool?
faq_plan.a: Yes, once they are approved. An app built on Emergent connects to any accounting or invoicing tool with an API and syncs approved hours to it. Unsigned weeks stay out. The invoice built from those hours is a separate decision: an invoice approval workflow handles who signs it before it goes to the client.

faq_plan.q: What should a timesheet approval workflow check before a manager sees the week?
faq_plan.a: It should check whatever a manager would otherwise catch by eye. Start with four: an empty workday with no leave logged, a weekly total under the hours you expect, a project code that is no longer open, and hours on a project the employee is not assigned to. Keep the list short, since every extra check is one more reason a correct week comes back.

faq_plan.q: What should a timesheet approval workflow do when the manager is on leave?
faq_plan.a: It should send the team's weeks to a backup the manager named in advance, for the dates the manager is away. If no backup is named, send the week to the manager's own manager rather than leaving it open. Because Emergent has no per-approver seats, naming a backup for every manager adds none.

faq_plan.q: Can a timesheet approval workflow flag hours over a project's budget?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The app can read the hours budgeted for each project from your project tracker and compare them with the hours logged to date. A week that takes a project past its budgeted hours goes to the project lead with the overrun shown. Approving the budget itself is a different job, covered by a budget approval workflow.

faq_plan.q: How do I add client sign-off to a timesheet approval workflow for contractors?
faq_plan.a: Store the client contact on each placement, and route the contractor's weekly timesheet to that person instead of an internal manager. The client approves the week or returns it with a comment. Emergent builds the email reminders too, and the app can nudge the client contact each day the week sits unsigned.

faq_plan.q: How long should a timesheet approval workflow wait before sending a reminder?
faq_plan.a: Wait one workday after submission before the first reminder, and escalate to the backup after a second day. Set the window per approver group: a client contact may need longer than an internal lead. Leave enough time before your payroll cutoff to fix a week that comes back.

faq_plan.q: Should a timesheet approval workflow send rejected weeks back to the employee?
faq_plan.a: Yes. It should return a rejected week to the employee, with a comment on the line that needs changing, because only the employee can correct their own hours. The approver sees the week again after the fix. The same return-with-comment step fits any approval workflow, where a request goes back to the person who made it.

plan.angle: The top results define timesheet approval as one employee, one manager, one approve button. This page builds the four routing problems that make a timesheet approval workflow hard in practice: one week of hours split across two projects with two different leads, a contractor's week that the client has to sign before it counts, a week with a missing day that goes back to the employee before any manager sees it, and a manager on leave whose team still needs a named backup approver. Overtime review, raises and pay-run cutoffs belong to the payroll automation page and generic routing to the approval workflow page; this page stays on getting submitted hours approved by the right person.
